prompt: Match each part of a decision record to the question it answers for a later reader.
hint: Status is about now; context is about then.

pairs.right: what was true, and what pulled each way?
what became true because of it?

prompt: Which of these decisions deserve a full record by the lesson's test? Choose all that apply.
hint: Expensive to reverse, and affecting more than the people who made it.

choices.text: Moving seat holds out of the booking database
choices.why: Yes: structural, cross-team, and expensive to reverse.

choices.text: Choosing the message broker for ticket events
choices.why: Yes: technology with a long tail that several teams build on.

choices.text: Upgrading a JSON library by a minor version
choices.why: Cheap to reverse and local; a log full of these is a log nobody reads.

choices.text: A question answered twice in chat about why Frota is read nightly
choices.why: Yes: if people keep asking, the third answer should be a link.

prompt: How does the lesson separate a decision record from a design document?
hint: One explores; the other closes.

choices.text: One closes a question, the other keeps exploring
choices.why: Right: a record closes one decision; a design document explores and evolves, and long ones produce several records as their conclusions settle.

choices.text: A record is longer and more formal
choices.why: The opposite: most records are a page.

choices.text: A design document is written after the code ships
choices.why: Design documents usually come first; the difference is in what they do, not when.

choices.text: Architects alone may write records
choices.why: Anybody who owns the decision writes it; the architect makes sure it gets written.

prompt: A context section says: We need a fast in-memory store for seat holds. What is wrong with it?
hint: Could a reader imagine choosing differently?

choices.text: It is too short to be useful to a reader
choices.why: Length is not the issue; a short force can be excellent.

choices.text: It is the decision, written early
choices.why: Yes: the solution in disguise makes the options look like theatre.

choices.text: It names no technology
choices.why: Naming one would make it worse: it would be the decision with a brand on it.

choices.text: It belongs under consequences instead
choices.why: It is not a consequence either; it is the answer stated as a need.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer 85% CPU at peak in June 2025 to the database is busy?
hint: Forces age.

choices.text: Because auditors require numbers
choices.why: The reason given is for the next reader, not an auditor.

choices.text: Because numbers make the record look more serious
choices.why: The point is checkability, not appearance.

choices.text: A later reader compares it with today's dashboard
choices.why: Right: the number and the date say how far the forces have moved since.

choices.text: Because busy is an informal word
choices.why: Informality is not the problem; vagueness is.

prompt: At peak, Carcará created 1,800 seat holds a minute and 70% of them expired unpaid. How many holds expired each minute?
hint: Seventy per cent of the holds.

prompt: Why are the decision drivers fixed before the options are compared?
hint: What happens to a comparison with no fixed criteria?

choices.text: Because MADR lists them first
choices.why: The order in a template follows from the reason; it is not the reason.

choices.text: To keep the number of options small
choices.why: Drivers do not limit options; they are the yardstick for all of them.

choices.text: Because drivers are frozen once the record is accepted
choices.why: True of the whole record, and not why they come first.

choices.text: So the comparison stays off the favourite
choices.why: Yes: fixing the criteria first stops the comparison drifting toward the author's favourite, where each option is judged on the criterion it happens to win.

prompt: In the seat-hold comparison, option A is to keep holds in PostgreSQL. How does the lesson ask you to write its case?
hint: As its supporters would.

choices.text: As standing still, since the code stays the same
choices.why: That is the straw man the lesson warns against.

choices.text: As the simplest system, with nothing new
choices.why: Right: a real strength, which the table should show.

choices.text: Briefly, because it was rejected
choices.why: Rejected options are exactly what a successor needs to see argued fairly.

choices.text: It should be left out of the record
choices.why: Leaving it out invites somebody to rediscover it as a new idea.

prompt: Forty passengers lose their seats when Redis restarts during a deploy. How does the record of the decision help?
hint: What did the negative consequence say?

choices.text: It names who to blame
choices.why: Records describe forces and trade-offs, not culprits.

choices.text: It shows the restart was a mistake to allow
choices.why: The record expected restarts; it does not forbid them.

choices.text: A known cost, accepted for stated reasons
choices.why: Yes: without it, the incident reads as a mistake and the decision gets reversed in a hurry.

choices.text: It contains the steps to restore the holds
choices.why: Implementation and recovery steps belong in a runbook, not in the record.

prompt: Which of these belong in the consequences of the seat-hold record? Choose all that apply.
hint: What became true, good and bad, and checkable.

choices.text: Booking database CPU falls below 60% at peak
choices.why: Yes: a positive consequence, specific enough to check.

choices.text: A Redis restart loses the holds in flight
choices.why: Yes: the negative one that protects the decision later.

choices.text: Create the Redis client and add a feature flag on Tuesday
choices.why: That is a plan; link to the ticket instead.

choices.text: We will use Redis for holds
choices.why: That restates the decision; it is not a consequence of it.

prompt: ADR-0004 decided to keep holds in the database; two years later, holds move to Redis. What should happen to ADR-0004?
hint: An accepted record is never rewritten.

choices.text: Edit it to say Redis, so the log matches the code
choices.why: That destroys the history of why the answer changed.

choices.text: Delete it, as it no longer applies to the code
choices.why: Deleting loses the reasoning a successor needs before proposing the old approach again.

choices.text: Set its status to deprecated
choices.why: Deprecated means nothing replaces it; here something does.

choices.text: Mark it superseded by the new record
choices.why: Right: both records stay, each true about its own time.

prompt: Match each status to its meaning.
hint: One means replaced; another means gone with nothing in its place.

pairs.right: open for comment, text still changing
no longer applies, nothing replaces it

prompt: A record's title is improved two years after it was accepted. What must not change?
hint: Its stable identity.

choices.text: The file's text formatting
choices.why: Typos and formatting may be fixed; the decision and its number may not change.

choices.text: Its number
choices.why: Right: numbers are never reused or changed; other records and code comments point at them.

choices.text: The links to evidence
choices.why: Fixing a broken link is one of the edits an accepted record may receive.

choices.text: The folder it lives in
choices.why: Not ideal to move, and still not the identity the lesson names.

prompt: In ADR-0014, why does option B, holding every seat for 30 minutes, lose?
hint: Who pays for it, and how often?

choices.text: It makes late approvals rarer, not impossible
choices.why: True, and still not the cost the record weighs; even option C does not make them impossible.

choices.text: Every passenger pays for longer holds
choices.why: Yes: every passenger would wait behind 30-minute holds on seats others abandoned, a cost on every purchase to avoid a 0.4% case that option C handles directly.

choices.text: The payment gateway forbids holds over ten minutes
choices.why: The gateway knows nothing about Carcará's holds.

choices.text: It moves a passenger who did no wrong
choices.why: That is option A's flaw.

prompt: ADR-0014's last consequence says the state machine gains a transition. Why does the lesson point at it?
hint: Decisions and models have to agree.

choices.text: Behaviour changed, so the diagrams must too
choices.why: Right, and saying so in the record makes the update part of the decision.

choices.text: Because consequences are required to name a diagram
choices.why: There is no such rule; it matters here because behaviour changed.

choices.text: Because the state machine is the record's appendix
choices.why: It is a separate artefact that the record keeps consistent.

choices.text: To make the record longer
choices.why: Length is never the aim.

prompt: A Y-statement ends with the line ___ <the downside>, and if you cannot fill it in you have not found the decision's cost.
hint: The last of its six lines.

prompt: Match each decision to the weight of record the lesson suggests.
hint: The wider and less reversible, the heavier.

pairs.left: moving holds out of the booking database
a team choosing a date format for its own API
pairs.right: a Y-statement or a row in a decision table

pairs.left: sorting in memory in one function

right_distractors: an e-mail to the whole company

prompt: Put Carcará's steps for proposing a record in order.
hint: The merge is the moment it becomes accepted.
items: Write the record as Proposed and open a pull request
Ask the owners of what it changes to review it
Discuss in the pull request and improve the text
Merge with the status set to Accepted and the date
trap: Merging first and discussing later turns the review into a formality.

prompt: Which reason does the lesson give for keeping records in the repository rather than a wiki?
hint: Check out last year's code.

choices.text: Wikis are not allowed by the security team
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: Repositories search better than a wiki does
choices.why: Not the argument; the argument is about being found, versioned and reviewed.

choices.text: Old code then comes with its old decisions
choices.why: Yes: records are versioned with the code, so checking out old code checks out its decisions; they are also found beside the code and reviewed like it.

choices.text: Tools like adr-tools require it
choices.why: The tools are optional and work on plain files anywhere.

prompt: Bento proposes moving seat holds back to PostgreSQL, because one store is simpler. What should Tainá point him to first?
hint: The log was written for exactly this moment.

choices.text: The Redis documentation
choices.why: It explains Redis, not why Carcará chose it.

choices.text: ADR-0004 and ADR-0009, then today's numbers
choices.why: Right: the original decision, why it stopped working, and whether those forces still hold.

choices.text: The code that calls Redis
choices.why: The code says what; the records say why.

choices.text: The incident report from the Redis restart
choices.why: One cost the decision already accepted; the records give the whole trade-off.
